paragraphs.text: Loose [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) made in 1976 from leaf grown in Menghai County, Yunnan. The county named on a label is a different claim from [Menghai Tea Factory](menghai-county:county-and-factory), which blends leaf from several of the county’s mountains. The leaf was fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making), rolled and dried in the sun into maocha, then [left loose](sheng:processing) rather than pressed. It is never dried with hot air afterwards, so some of the leaf’s own activity survives, and that is what lets it keep changing for years.

At fifty years it sits well past the point where the trade starts calling raw pu’er [aged](sheng:ageing): some set that at ten years, and many wait for twenty or more. Raw pu’er does not get shou’s quick fermentation, so it changes only [through storage](sheng:aging), and [heat and humidity](sheng:storage) decide how fast. Its five decades of keeping are part of its history as much as its age.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
